title: Margin, PDT, settlement, cash
teaches: Know the account rules before they bite: what margin lends and when it calls, how FINRA replaced the pattern day trader rule in 2026, how T+1 settlement trips up a cash account, and why going to cash is a trade with a cost.

facts.quote: new intraday margin standards to replace in their entirety the outdated day trading margin requirements, including the day trade count requirements for designating a customer as a “pattern day trader” and the $25,000 pattern day trader minimum equity requirement
facts.claim: FINRA's new intraday margin standards replace the old day trading rules entirely, the pattern day trader trade count and the $25,000 minimum included.

facts.quote: Effective Date: June 4, 2026; Phase-in Period: Ends October 20, 2027
facts.claim: The new rule took effect June 4, 2026, and brokers may phase it in until October 20, 2027.

facts.quote: Members that need more time to implement the rule change will be permitted to phase in their implementation over a period of 18 months, until October 20, 2027.
facts.claim: Brokers that need more time can take up to 18 months to switch.

facts.quote: The new rule does not change the regular maintenance margin requirements as they exist today, but rather supplements them.
facts.claim: The regular maintenance margin rules stay the same; the intraday rule adds to them.

facts.quote: There’s no $25,000 minimum equity requirement for day trading.
facts.claim: Under the new rule there is no $25,000 minimum to day trade.

facts.quote: There’s no "pattern day trader" designation based on counting trades. Instead, your firm monitors your account to ensure you maintain adequate equity during the trading day relative to your actual positions.
facts.claim: The new rule drops the trade count and checks your equity against your positions during the day.

facts.quote: If an imbalance occurs and your account doesn’t have enough equity to cover your open positions, you have an "intraday margin deficit" that you're expected to satisfy as promptly as possible.
facts.claim: Too little equity for your open positions during the day is an intraday margin deficit, and you must cover it promptly.

facts.quote: If you repeatedly fail to satisfy intraday margin deficits promptly, this may result in your account being restricted for up to 90 days.
facts.claim: Repeatedly missing intraday margin deficits can get the account restricted for up to 90 days.

facts.quote: Your firm might continue operating under the old day trading margin requirements during the transition, or they might choose to migrate to the new system sooner.
facts.claim: During the transition, your broker may still run the old day trading rules.

facts.quote: However, $2,000 is the minimum equity required to engage in leveraged trading (trading on margin).
facts.claim: You need at least $2,000 of equity to borrow on margin.

facts.quote: You can trade in a margin account with less than $2,000 in equity, but you cannot use leverage—you must trade only with the cash you have available
facts.claim: Under $2,000 of equity you can still trade in a margin account, but only with your own cash.

facts.quote: you must hold adequate maintenance margin—a minimum equity level of 25 percent of the current market value of the long margin-eligible equity securities in your margin account—throughout the entire trading day, not just at end of the day.
facts.claim: Under the new rule, the 25% maintenance level applies all through the trading day, not just at the close.

facts.quote: Your firm has the authority to impose higher requirements if they choose.
facts.claim: Your broker can set higher requirements than FINRA's.

facts.quote: When you buy securities in a cash account, you must pay for securities in full before selling them.
facts.claim: In a cash account, you pay in full before you sell.

facts.quote: You can also incur what’s known as a “good faith violation” if you purchase a security with cash from a transaction that hasn’t settled yet and then sell the security before the proceeds used to fund the purchase have settled.
facts.claim: Buying with unsettled cash and selling before that cash settles is a good faith violation.

facts.quote: The current settlement time for most equity trades is T+1, or the next business day.
facts.claim: Most stock trades settle T+1, the next business day.

facts.quote: if you want to engage in intraday trading in a cash account, be sure that you fully pay for those securities at the time of purchase with settled funds.
facts.claim: To day trade in a cash account, pay for each buy with settled cash.

facts.quote: To trade using margin (funds borrowed from your firm), you must maintain a minimum of $2,000 in equity in your margin account.
facts.claim: Trading on margin needs at least $2,000 of equity in the account.

facts.quote: Your brokerage firm may require higher minimum equity amounts—often called "house" requirements—depending on the firm's policies and your account activity.
facts.claim: Brokers can require more equity than FINRA's minimum; these are house requirements.

facts.quote: However, margin trading comes with its own set of risks, including the potential to lose more than your original investment.
facts.claim: On margin you can lose more than you put in.

facts.quote: A margin account allows you to borrow money from a brokerage firm to buy securities. This is also the only type of account in which investors can engage in short selling.
facts.claim: A margin account lets you borrow to buy, and it is the only account that allows short selling.

facts.quote: You may also enter into a short sale through a margin account, which involves you borrowing stock from a firm in order to sell it, hoping that the price will decline.
facts.claim: A short sale borrows stock to sell it, and it goes through a margin account.

facts.quote: In general, under Federal Reserve Board Regulation T, firms can lend a customer up to 50 percent of the total purchase price of a stock for new, or initial, purchases.
facts.claim: Under Regulation T, a broker can lend up to half the price of a new stock purchase.

facts.quote: Under these rules, as a general matter, your equity in the account must not fall below 25 percent of the current market value of the securities in the account.
facts.claim: FINRA's maintenance floor: your equity must stay at or above 25% of the stocks' current value.

facts.quote: your account equity would fall to $10,000 ($60,000 market value minus $50,000 loan amount).
facts.claim: Equity is the market value minus the margin loan.

facts.quote: Since the required equity is $15,000, your firm will likely issue a maintenance margin call for $5,000 ($15,000 less existing equity of $10,000).
facts.claim: The margin call is the required equity minus the equity you have.

facts.quote: Brokerage firms have the right to set their own maintenance margin requirements—often called "house" requirements—as long as they’re more stringent than the margin requirements under FINRA rules.
facts.claim: Brokers can set maintenance requirements stricter than FINRA's.

facts.quote: These changes in firm policy often take effect immediately and may result in the issuance of a maintenance margin call.
facts.claim: A broker's higher requirement can take effect at once and trigger a margin call.

facts.quote: You can lose more funds than you deposit in the margin account.
facts.claim: On margin you can lose more than you deposit.

facts.quote: The firm can sell your securities without notice.
facts.claim: The broker can sell your securities without telling you.

facts.quote: As a matter of customer relations, most firms will attempt to notify their customers of margin calls, but they aren’t required to do so.
facts.claim: Most brokers try to tell you about a margin call, but they don't have to.

facts.quote: You’re not entitled to an extension of time on a margin call.
facts.claim: You have no right to extra time on a margin call.

facts.quote: A firm charges interest for the money it lends its customers to purchase securities on margin
facts.claim: Margin interest is charged on the money the broker lends you.

facts.quote: With a cash account, you’re expected to pay the full amount for all securities purchased by the settlement date—which, for most securities, including options, means paying for them one day after you place an order to buy.
facts.claim: In a cash account, payment is due by settlement, one day after the buy, options included.

facts.quote: To estimate the potential loss in market value before incurring a maintenance call, use this formula: Current Maintenance Margin Excess ÷ (1.00 - maintenance requirement percentage)
facts.claim: FINRA's formula for how much value you can lose before a maintenance call: the margin excess divided by one minus the maintenance percent.

facts.quote: Some securities cannot be purchased on margin, which means they must be paid for in full
facts.claim: Some securities can't be bought on margin at all.

facts.quote: 25 percent of the current market value of all margin securities
facts.claim: Rule 4210's maintenance margin for long margin stocks is 25% of their current market value.

facts.quote: computed by adding the current market value of all securities "long" and the amount of any credit balance and subtracting the current market value of all securities "short" and the amount of any debit balance
facts.claim: Equity is what you own minus what you owe, including the margin loan (the debit balance).

facts.quote: Under the T+1 settlement cycle, most securities transactions settle on the next business day following their transaction date.
facts.claim: Under T+1, most trades settle the next business day.

facts.quote: For example, if you sell shares of a stock on Tuesday, the transaction will settle on Wednesday.
facts.claim: Sell on Tuesday and the sale settles Wednesday.

facts.quote: The T+1 settlement cycle applies to transactions for stocks, bonds, options, municipal securities, exchange-traded funds, certain mutual funds and U.S. government securities, and limited partnerships that trade on an exchange.
facts.claim: T+1 covers stocks, options, ETFs and bonds alike.

facts.quote: As of May 2024, the standard for settlement is next business day after a trade, or T+1.
facts.claim: Since May 2024, the standard settlement is T+1.

facts.quote: Since 2017, the settlement cycle – the time between the transaction date and the settlement date – for most securities transactions has been two business days – often referred to as “T+2.”
facts.claim: Before T+1, most trades settled in two business days (T+2).

facts.quote: The new “T+1” settlement cycle will apply to all applicable securities transactions occurring on or after May 28, 2024.
facts.claim: T+1 started with trades on or after May 28, 2024.

facts.quote: FINRA rules define a “pattern day trader” as any customer who executes four or more “day trades” within five business days
facts.claim: Under the old rule, four or more day trades in five business days made you a pattern day trader.

facts.quote: provided that the number of day trades represents more than six percent of the customer’s total trades in the margin account for that same five business day period.
facts.claim: The old count also required day trades to be more than 6% of your trades in the margin account in those five days.

facts.quote: Under FINRA rules, customers designated “pattern day traders” by their brokerage firms must have at least $25,000 in their accounts and can only trade in margin accounts.
facts.claim: Under the old rule, a pattern day trader needed at least $25,000, in a margin account.

facts.quote: The new intraday margin requirements, effective June 4, 2026, permit a transition period until October 20, 2027, for brokerage firms that need more time to comply.
facts.claim: The SEC's investor site confirms the change took effect June 4, 2026, with a transition to October 20, 2027.

facts.quote: If an investor buys and sells a security before paying for it, the investor is “freeriding”
facts.claim: Buying and selling before you pay is freeriding.

facts.quote: which is not permitted under the Federal Reserve Board’s Regulation T and may require the investor’s broker to “freeze” the investor’s cash account for 90 days.
facts.claim: Freeriding breaks Regulation T and can get the cash account frozen for 90 days.

facts.quote: During this 90-day period, an investor may still purchase securities with the cash account, but the investor must fully pay for any purchase on the date of the trade.
facts.claim: During a freeze you can still buy, but you pay in full on the trade date.

facts.quote: your brokerage firm can require you to deposit cash or securities to your account immediately, or sell any of the securities in your account to cover any shortfall, without informing you in advance.
facts.claim: On a margin call, the broker can demand money at once or sell your holdings without warning.

facts.quote: Even if the brokerage firm notifies you that you have a certain number of days to cover the shortfall, it still may sell your securities before then.
facts.claim: Even after giving you days to pay, the broker can sell sooner.

facts.quote: Margin increases investors’ purchasing power, but also exposes investors to the potential for larger losses.
facts.claim: Margin raises buying power and the size of possible losses.

facts.quote: 50 percent of the current market value of the security or the percentage set by the regulatory authority where the trade occurs, whichever is greater.
facts.claim: Regulation T's margin on a margin stock is 50% of its current value.

facts.quote: A good faith violation occurs when you buy a security and sell it before paying for the initial purchase in full with settled funds. Only cash or the sales proceeds of fully paid for securities qualify as "settled funds."
facts.claim: Selling a stock before it was paid for with settled funds is a good faith violation.

facts.quote: If Marty sells ABC stock prior to Tuesday (the settlement date of the XYZ sale), the transaction would be deemed a good faith violation
facts.claim: Fidelity's example: buy with Monday's sale proceeds and sell before they settle Tuesday, and it's a violation.

facts.quote: This trade is a violation because Trudy sold ABC before Monday's sale of XYZ stock settled and those proceeds became available to pay for the purchase of ABC stock
facts.claim: Starting the day with settled cash doesn't help: reusing a same-day sale and selling again that day is a violation.

facts.quote: If you incur three good faith violations in a 12-month period in a cash account, your brokerage firm will restrict your account.
facts.claim: At Fidelity, three good faith violations in 12 months restricts the cash account.

facts.quote: This means you will only be able to buy securities if you have sufficient settled cash in the account prior to placing a trade. This restriction will be effective for 90 calendar days.
facts.claim: The restriction means settled cash before every buy, for 90 days.

facts.quote: A freeriding violation occurs because Marty did not pay for the stock in full prior to selling it.
facts.claim: Selling a stock you never paid for is freeriding.

facts.quote: Making new buys in a correction is riskier, since most stocks will follow the market's downward trend.
facts.claim: New buys in a correction are riskier because most stocks follow the market down.

facts.quote: Use this time to look for stocks to add to your watch list so you'll be ready to take action when the market starts a new uptrend.
facts.claim: In a correction, build your watch list for the next uptrend.

facts.quote: Your goal is to make money when the market is trending higher and to protect your profits when it starts heading lower.
facts.claim: Make money in uptrends and protect it when the market turns down.

facts.quote: if the overall market is in a downtrend, it will be very hard for even the best stocks to move higher.
facts.claim: In a market downtrend, even the best stocks struggle to rise.

facts.quote: The biggest risk of market timing is usually considered not being in the market at critical times. Investors who try to time the market run the risk of missing periods of exceptional returns.
facts.claim: Being out of the market can mean missing its best stretches.

facts.quote: if an investor moves their money out of stocks during a market downturn, they risk not moving their money back in time to take advantage of gains from an upswing.
facts.claim: Go to cash in a downturn and you risk missing the upswing.

facts.quote: And they often end as abruptly as they began, with a quick rebound that is very difficult to predict
facts.claim: Bear markets often end with a quick rebound that is hard to predict.

facts.quote: Investors use a "cash is king" strategy when securities prices in the market are high and opt to save cash for when prices become cheaper.
facts.claim: Holding cash can be a deliberate choice, saved for better prices.

facts.quote: As a form of investment, it is important to not let cash sit idle but rather to invest so that returns are at least equal to inflation.
facts.claim: Idle cash loses ground to inflation over time.

facts.quote: CANSLIM stocks can quickly decline if the market shifts and institutional investors move to safer assets.
facts.claim: Growth leaders can fall fast when the market turns.

facts.quote: CANSLIM stocks tend to be over-performers in bull markets.
facts.claim: Growth stocks do their best work in bull markets.

facts.quote: However, investors must still weigh the risks involved with purchases, as they could well see a further decline as the correction continues.
facts.claim: Buying in a correction risks a further decline as it continues.

facts.quote: a dramatic correction that occurs in the course of one trading session can be disastrous for a short-term or day trader and those traders who are extremely leveraged.
facts.claim: A sharp correction can be disastrous for short-term traders on heavy margin.

facts.quote: A “margin account” is a type of brokerage account in which the broker-dealer lends the investor cash, using the account as collateral, to purchase securities.
facts.claim: In a margin account, the broker lends you cash to buy, with your account as collateral.

facts.quote: An investor using a cash account is not allowed to borrow funds from his or her broker-dealer in order to pay for transactions in the account
facts.claim: A cash account can't borrow from the broker.

facts.quote: No setup, no trade: never force a trade to have something on; cash is a position.
facts.claim: Our rule: never force a trade; cash is a position.

facts.quote: All positions together: up to 200% of the account in a Green market (margin, B24, F60), up to 100% otherwise
facts.claim: Our rule: all positions together can reach 200% of the account in a Green market, 100% otherwise.

facts.quote: Margin (up to 200%, B24) is used only in a Green market.
facts.claim: Our rule: margin is used only in a Green market.

facts.quote: Max position 40% of the account
facts.claim: Our rule: one position is at most 40% of the account.

facts.quote: Margin: total long positions up to 200% of the account. Risk per trade is still a percent of the account.
facts.claim: Our rule: on margin, longs can reach 200% of the account, and risk per trade stays a percent of the account.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider.
facts.claim: Our rule: the stop is the exit, and it only moves up.

facts.quote: A market filter decides when the account trades: the app's market reading (Green, Yellow, Orange, Red).
facts.claim: Our market filter is the app's market reading: Green, Yellow, Orange or Red.

walkthroughs.title: Margin is a loan
steps: Margin is your broker lending you money to buy. Under Regulation T, it can lend up to half of a new buy.
Then there's a floor. Your equity can't drop under 25% of what the stocks are worth. Your broker's line can be higher.
Break it and you get a margin call. They can sell your stock without even telling you first.
And the loan cuts both ways. It grows your losses too, and you can lose more than you put in.

walkthroughs.title: The day trading rule changed
steps: Old rule: four or more day trades in five business days, and you're a pattern day trader. That meant $25,000 minimum.
FINRA scrapped it June 4, 2026. No trade count, no $25,000. Now your equity has to cover your positions all day.
Brokers have until October 20, 2027 to switch over. So ask yours which rules your account runs on today.

walkthroughs.title: Settled cash in a cash account
steps: Most trades settle T+1, the next business day. Sell Tuesday, and that cash is yours Wednesday.
Buy with cash that hasn't settled, then sell before it does. That's a good faith violation.
Buy and sell before you've paid at all, and that's freeriding. Your broker can freeze the account for 90 days.

questions.q: Your broker offers to switch your cash account to margin. What does that actually let you do?
choices: Borrow from your broker to buy
Cap your loss at what you deposit
Buy any stock with no money down
Hold shares safe from forced sales
questions.answer: Borrow from your broker to buy
questions.why: You borrow from your broker to buy. The broker lends you cash, and your account backs the loan. Under Regulation T it can lend up to 50% of a new stock buy. Some stocks can't be bought on margin at all. Here's the part people forget. The loan cuts both ways. It grows your buying power, and it grows your losses. You can lose more than you put in. We only use margin when the app's market reading is Green.
questions.lesson_line: Margin's a loan. It makes your winners bigger and your losers bigger.

wrong.Cap your loss at what you deposit: Backwards. On margin you can lose more than you put in. That's the whole danger of it.
wrong.Buy any stock with no money down: You put up part of every new buy yourself, and some stocks can't be bought on margin at all.
wrong.Hold shares safe from forced sales: Backwards. Fall short and your broker can sell your shares without telling you.

questions.simple: Margin is a loan from your broker, backed by your account. It grows your buying power and your losses.

reasons: fixed before (checker split a wrong note)

questions.q: You're on margin and you get a margin call. Your broker can sell your shares to cover it without reaching you first.
questions.why: True, and people get burned by this. Your broker doesn't have to reach you before it sells. FINRA and the SEC both say so. Most brokers will try to tell you about a call, but they don't have to. Even if you're given a few days to pay, they can still sell sooner. So don't sit waiting on an email. Watch your equity yourself, and cover a call right away.
questions.lesson_line: A margin call isn't a conversation. Watch your equity so the broker never has to.
questions.simple: True. Your broker can sell your shares to cover a call, and it doesn't have to reach you first.

deeper.trap: A note from your broker giving you a few days to cover a call is not a promise. The SEC says the broker may still sell your securities before then. Plan to meet a call at once.

questions.q: You're holding stock on margin. How low can your equity sit, as a share of what the stocks are worth, before you're under FINRA's floor?
questions.sentence: Your equity must stay at or above ___ of what your stocks are worth right now.
questions.why: 25%. Your equity is what's yours after you take away the loan. FINRA says it can't drop below 25% of what the stocks are worth today. That's maintenance margin, and it's a floor, not a target. Your broker can set it higher, and its number is the one that calls you. So look up your broker's maintenance number before you borrow. Don't mix it up with the 50% Regulation T lets you borrow on a new buy.
questions.lesson_line: Know your broker's maintenance number. FINRA's 25% is just the floor.
questions.simple: 25%. FINRA won't let your equity fall below that share of what your stocks are worth, and brokers can ask for more.

reasons: a rule number FINRA sets and could change

questions.q: Before you buy on margin: under Regulation T, how much of a new stock buy can your broker lend you?
questions.why: Up to 50%. Regulation T lets the broker lend up to half the price of a new stock buy. The other half is your money. That limit is only for getting in. Once you own it, the line to watch is FINRA's 25% maintenance floor. So 50% to get in, 25% to stay in.
questions.lesson_line: 50% to get in, 25% to stay in.

wrong.Up to 25%: Mixed up the two numbers. 25% is the equity you have to keep after the buy, not the loan.
wrong.Up to 75%: Too much. Regulation T caps the loan on a new buy at half the price.
wrong.Up to 100%: That's buying with none of your own money. At least half of every new buy is yours.

questions.simple: Up to half. Regulation T has you put up at least the other half of a new stock buy.

reasons: a rule number (Regulation T's 50%) that the Federal Reserve sets and could change

questions.q: It's November 2026. FINRA's margin rule still says you need $25,000 in the account to day trade.
questions.why: False. FINRA threw out the old day trading rules on June 4, 2026. The pattern day trader count and the $25,000 minimum went with them. Here's the catch. Brokers can phase the new rule in until October 20, 2027. So your broker might still hold you to $25,000 today. Don't go by the headline. Ask your broker which rules your account is on before you day trade a small account.
questions.lesson_line: FINRA dropped the $25,000 rule. Your broker might not have yet, so ask.
questions.simple: False. FINRA dropped the $25,000 minimum, but your broker may still use the old rule for a while.

reasons: a rule that changed in 2026, with a phase-in for brokers until October 20, 2027

questions.q: You sell a stock Thursday morning, and there's no holiday this week. When is that cash actually settled?
questions.why: Friday. Trades settle T+1 now, one business day after the trade. FINRA's own example is a Tuesday sale settling Wednesday, so Thursday's sale settles Friday. Why you care: in a cash account, that money isn't free to trade in and out with until it settles. Before May 28, 2024 it took two business days, which would've meant Monday.
questions.lesson_line: Trade day plus one business day. That's when the cash is really yours.

wrong.Thursday, the same day: That's the trade date. Settlement comes one business day later.
wrong.The next Monday: That's two business days, the old T+2. T+1 took over on May 28, 2024.
wrong.The next Thursday: Way too long. A Thursday sale settles Friday.

questions.simple: Friday. Trades settle one business day after you make them.

reasons: a settlement cycle that changed in 2024 and could change again

questions.q: A stock on your list just broke below its 200-day and you want to short it. Which account lets you do that?
questions.why: A margin account. When you short, you borrow shares from your broker and sell them, hoping to buy them back lower. FINRA says a margin account is the only kind that allows that. A cash account can't borrow anything, so it can't short. If you ever plan to short, set up margin ahead of time, not the day the chart breaks.
questions.lesson_line: No margin account, no shorting.

wrong.A cash account: A cash account can't borrow from the broker, and a short sells borrowed shares.
wrong.Either one works: Only margin works. The shares you sell short are borrowed.
wrong.An options account: Options approval doesn't let you short shares. Shorting means borrowing them, and that takes margin.

questions.simple: A margin account. A short sells borrowed shares, and only a margin account can borrow.

questions.q: You buy calls in a cash account on Monday. The money for them is due Tuesday, one business day later, just like stock.
questions.why: True. Options settle T+1 too. FINRA puts stocks, options, ETFs and bonds on the same one-day cycle. So in a cash account the money for Monday's calls is due Tuesday, same as a stock. It works the other way too. Sell those calls and the cash isn't settled until the next business day.
questions.lesson_line: Stock or option, it all settles the next business day.
questions.simple: True. Options settle one business day after the trade, the same as stock.

reasons: a settlement cycle that changed in 2024 and could change again

questions.q: $20,000 of stock, bought with a $10,000 margin loan, is now worth $12,500. Where's your equity, as a percent of its value?
questions.why: 20%, so expect a margin call. Your equity is the value minus the loan. $12,500 minus $10,000 is $2,500. $2,500 over $12,500 is 0.2, so 20%. FINRA's floor is 25%, and your broker's may be higher. Here's what bites people. The loan never shrinks when the stock falls, so the whole drop comes out of your equity. That's why I check equity as a percent, not just dollars.
questions.lesson_line: Equity is value minus loan. On margin, check it as a percent every day.
questions.simple: 20%. The loan stayed the same while the stock fell, so your equity sank under FINRA's floor.

reasons: computed key (calc margin_equity_pct)

wrong.80%: That's the loan's share of the value. You want the part that's yours.
wrong.12.5%: Divided the $2,500 by the $20,000 you paid. Use what it's worth now.
wrong.50%: That's where you started. The drop came out of your equity, not the loan.

questions.q: Cash account. You buy A with settled cash, sell it, then buy B with that money. Selling B today is fine.
questions.why: False. Selling A was fine, because you paid for A with settled cash. B is the problem. You paid for B with the money from A's sale, and that money doesn't settle until the next business day. Sell B before then and you've sold a stock bought with unsettled cash. That's a good faith violation. The fix is simple. Hold B until A's sale settles, or pay for B with cash that's already settled.
questions.lesson_line: Settled cash can do one round trip. Today's sale money can't, until it settles.
questions.simple: False. B was bought with A's sale money, which hasn't settled, so selling B today is a violation.

deeper.trap: Starting the day with settled cash protects only the buys that cash paid for. In Fidelity's example, Trudy sold ABC before Monday's sale of ZQRT settled, and that was a violation. Each time you reuse cash from a same-day sale, hold what it buys until that cash settles.

reasons: fixed before (rebuilt by the checker on Fidelity's Trudy case)

questions.q: Your margin account has $1,500 of equity. How much does FINRA want to see before you can borrow on margin?
questions.why: $2,000. FINRA wants at least $2,000 of equity before you can trade on margin. At $1,500 you can still trade in that account, just with your own cash. No borrowing. Your broker can ask for more, so check its minimum too. And don't mix this up with $25,000. That was the old pattern day trader minimum, and it was never the line to borrow.
questions.lesson_line: $2,000 to borrow. Your broker's number may be higher.

wrong.$25,000: That was the old day trading minimum, never the line to borrow, and FINRA's dropped it.
wrong.No minimum at all: There's a floor. Under $2,000 you trade only with your own cash.
wrong.25% of the position: That's the equity you have to keep once you've borrowed. The line to borrow at all is $2,000.

questions.simple: $2,000 of equity. Under that you can still trade the account, but only with your own cash.

reasons: a dollar minimum FINRA sets and could change
fixed before (checker changed the $25,000 note)

questions.q: Margin call math: $40,000 of stock, a $20,000 loan, and it's fallen to $24,000. At FINRA's 25% floor, how big is the call?
questions.why: $2,000. Work out what you need, then what you have. You need 25% of $24,000, which is $6,000. You have $24,000 minus the $20,000 loan, which is $4,000. $6,000 minus $4,000 leaves you $2,000 short. That's the call. Pay it in cash and you're right back on the floor, so the next red day can call you again. Ask why you're that close to the line in the first place.
questions.lesson_line: The call is what you need minus what you have.
questions.simple: The call is the gap between the equity you need and the equity you have.

deeper.trap: Paying the call in cash only brings you back to the floor, so the next dip puts you under it again. FINRA's own example works the same way: required equity of $15,000 less equity of $10,000 is a $5,000 call.

reasons: computed key (calc arith)

wrong.$6,000: That's the equity you need. You never took off what you already have.
wrong.$4,000: That's the equity you have, not the gap.
wrong.$10,000: Took 25% of the old $40,000. The floor runs off what it's worth now.

questions.q: You put in $10,000 and borrow $10,000 to buy $20,000 of stock. It drops 30%. Ignoring interest, how much of your money is gone?
questions.why: 60%. The 30% drop hits the whole $20,000 position, and that's $6,000. The loan doesn't shrink, so all of it comes out of your $10,000. $6,000 over $10,000 is 0.6, so 60%. The stock fell 30% and you lost 60%. That's margin. It's why we only borrow when the app's market reading is Green.
questions.lesson_line: Borrow half and every drop hits your money twice as hard.
questions.simple: 60%. The whole drop comes out of your money, because the loan stays the same.

reasons: computed key (calc arith)

wrong.30%: That's the stock's drop. Your loss is twice that, because half the position was borrowed.
wrong.15%: Halved the loss because you borrowed half. The loan doesn't share the loss.
wrong.6%: Slipped a decimal. $6,000 out of $10,000 is 60%.

questions.story: Cash account, no settled cash. Monday morning you sell ZQRT. That afternoon you buy ABC with the money.
questions.q: When's the earliest you can sell ABC without a good faith violation?
choices: Right away, ZQRT is already sold
Only after you add new cash
questions.why: Tuesday, once ZQRT settles. You paid for ABC with ZQRT's sale money, and that money settles the next business day. Sell ABC before then and you've sold a stock bought with cash you didn't have yet. That's a good faith violation. Here's where it really hurts. Say ABC breaks down Monday afternoon. Now you're choosing between the violation and your stop. Keep settled cash on hand for your buys and you never face that choice.
questions.lesson_line: Bought with unsettled cash means you hold it until that cash settles.

wrong.Right away, ZQRT is already sold: Sold isn't settled. ZQRT's cash settles the next business day.
wrong.Only after you add new cash: No new money needed. ZQRT's proceeds pay for ABC once they settle.
wrong.Anytime after Monday's close: The close isn't settlement. ZQRT's sale settles the next business day, Tuesday.

questions.simple: Tuesday, once ZQRT's sale settles. ABC was paid for with that money.

reasons: rests on the T+1 settlement cycle, which changed in 2024

questions.story: Cash account with $0 in it. Monday you buy $5,000 of a stock and never send the money. Wednesday you sell it for $5,400 and use that to pay.
questions.q: What's your broker going to call this?
choices: A good faith violation on the sale
Nothing wrong, it made a profit
questions.why: Freeriding. You bought it and sold it without ever paying for it. Regulation T doesn't allow that, profit or not. Your broker can freeze the cash account for 90 days. During a freeze you can still buy, but you pay in full on the trade date. It's not a good faith violation. That one's when you paid with unsettled sale money. Here you never paid at all. Fund the account before you buy.
questions.lesson_line: Pay for it before you sell it, or risk a 90-day freeze.

wrong.A good faith violation on the sale: Close, but that's paying with unsettled sale money. You never paid at all.
wrong.Nothing wrong, it made a profit: Profit doesn't fix it. You sold it before you paid for it.
wrong.A pattern day trader violation: That old rule counted day trades in a margin account. You held from Monday to Wednesday in a cash account.

questions.simple: Freeriding. You sold the stock before you ever paid for it, and that can freeze the account.

questions.story: Your broker has switched to FINRA's new intraday margin rule. You day trade a few times a week in a $15,000 margin account.
questions.q: What's the new rule actually watching?
choices: Your day trades over five days
questions.why: Your equity against your positions, all day long. The new rule doesn't count your day trades, and it has no $25,000 minimum. So $15,000 isn't a problem by itself. What it watches is whether your equity covers what you're holding during the day. Come up short and that's an intraday margin deficit, which you cover fast. Miss them over and over and the account can be restricted for up to 90 days.
questions.lesson_line: The new rule doesn't count trades. Your equity has to cover your positions all day.

wrong.A $25,000 minimum balance: The new rule has no $25,000 minimum to day trade.
wrong.Nothing, trading is unlimited: Run short of equity and you owe an intraday margin deficit. Keep missing them and you get restricted.
wrong.Your day trades over five days: That was the old pattern day trader count. The new rule doesn't count trades.

questions.simple: Whether your equity covers your open positions during the day. No trade count and no $25,000 minimum.

reasons: a rule that changed in 2026 and that brokers may phase in until October 20, 2027

questions.story: $20,000 margin account. You make four day trades in five business days, and no other trades. Your broker still runs the old day trading rules.
questions.q: What happens to your account?
choices: Nothing until a fifth day trade
questions.why: You get flagged, and now you need $25,000 to keep day trading. Under the old rule, four or more day trades in five business days made you a pattern day trader. They also had to be more than six percent of your margin trades in that stretch. With no other trades, yours are all of them, and $20,000 is short of $25,000. Yes, FINRA dropped this rule. But your broker can keep running it until October 20, 2027. Go by your account, not the headline.
questions.lesson_line: Know which rules your broker runs. The old count still bites until it switches.

wrong.Nothing, FINRA dropped that rule: FINRA did, but your broker can phase it in. Until it switches, the old count applies.
wrong.Nothing until a fifth day trade: The old rule kicks in at four or more day trades in five business days.
wrong.Flagged, but $2,000 is enough: $2,000 is the line to borrow, not to day trade. A pattern day trader needed $25,000.

questions.simple: Flagged. Four day trades in five business days does it under the old rule, and then you need $25,000.

deeper.trap: The trap is going by the news, not your account. FINRA's new rule took effect June 4, 2026. A broker that needs more time may keep the old count until October 20, 2027. Until yours switches, the old count and the $25,000 minimum still apply to you.

reasons: a rule that changed in 2026; the key depends on the broker not having switched yet

questions.story: Cash account. Twice this month you bought with cash from a same-day sale. Both times the new stock hit its stop and you sold it that day.
questions.q: Which habit fixes this for good?
choices: Hold losers until the cash settles
Sell with a limit order instead
Keep to three trades a week
questions.why: Buy only with settled cash. Both of those trades were good faith violations. You bought with unsettled money, then sold before it settled. Pay for every buy with settled cash and your stop is always free to work. That's what matters. The stop is the exit, and you never want a rule keeping you in a loser. At Fidelity, three violations in 12 months gets you 90 days of buying with settled cash only. That count is Fidelity's, so check your own broker's.
questions.lesson_line: Trade a cash account with settled cash, so your stop is always free to work.

wrong.Hold losers until the cash settles: Now you're in a trade past your stop just to dodge a rule. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Sell with a limit order instead: The order type doesn't matter. Selling before the cash settles is the violation.
wrong.Keep to three trades a week: It's not a trade count. One buy with unsettled cash, sold before it settles, is a violation.

questions.simple: Only buy with settled cash. Then you can sell the second your stop hits, with no violation.

deeper.trap: The trap is holding the loser to dodge the violation. Now you're in a trade past your plan. The stop is the exit, so fix it before the buy and pay with settled cash.

reasons: fixed before (checker changed the question to ask for the best habit)
the three-in-12-months count is one broker's practice and can change

questions.q: Once your broker is on FINRA's new intraday rule, the 25% maintenance floor counts all day, not just at the close.
questions.why: True. On the new rule, the 25% floor covers the whole session, not just the close. Say a name you hold on margin flushes midday and bounces by the bell. Under the old way, only where you finished mattered. Now that midday low counts too. If your equity can't cover your positions during the day, that's an intraday margin deficit, and you cover it fast. Your broker can also set its number above 25%. So on margin, know where your equity sits through the day.
questions.lesson_line: On margin, watch your equity through the day, not just at the close.
questions.simple: True. On the new rule your equity has to stay at 25% or better all day, not just at the close.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking only the close counts. The 25% floor applies all through the trading day. If your equity can't cover your open positions during the day, that is an intraday margin deficit. You are expected to cover it as promptly as possible.

reasons: a rule that changed in 2026, with a broker phase-in

questions.story: You hold a volatile stock on margin, with equity at 35% of its value. Today your broker raises its requirement on that stock to 40%.
questions.q: What should you expect?
choices: A week's notice before any sale
questions.why: A margin call, today. Your broker can set its own requirement above FINRA's 25%, and a change can kick in at once. You're at 35% against a new 40%, so you're short right now. You're not owed extra time, and the broker can sell your shares without telling you. So on a volatile name, don't run your equity close to the line. Leave room for the broker to move it.
questions.lesson_line: FINRA's 25% is the floor. Your broker's number is the one that calls you.

wrong.Nothing, FINRA's floor is 25%: FINRA's 25% is the least a broker can ask. Your broker's number is the one you meet.
wrong.Nothing until your next buy: A new requirement can hit what you already hold, starting at once.
wrong.A week's notice before any sale: You're not owed extra time, and they can sell without telling you.

questions.simple: Expect a call right away. Your equity is now under your broker's new line.

deeper.trap: The trap is reading FINRA's 25% as the most a broker can ask for. It's the least. A broker can raise its own number, and the change can take effect at once. Know your broker's number on every stock you hold on margin.

questions.q: Say you buy $20,000 of stock with a $9,000 margin loan. How far can it fall before your equity hits FINRA's 25% floor?
questions.why: 40%. The $9,000 loan stays put while the stock falls. At the floor your equity is 0.25 of the value, so the loan is the other 0.75. $9,000 over 0.75 is $12,000. That's the value where you hit the floor. From $20,000 down to $12,000 is $8,000, and $8,000 over $20,000 is 0.4, so 40%. Do this before you borrow. Then you know exactly how much room you've got.
questions.lesson_line: Know the drop that triggers a margin call before you borrow, not after.
questions.simple: It can fall 40% before your equity hits the floor, because the loan stays the same as the stock drops.

deeper.trap: The trap is taking 25% of the $20,000 you paid. FINRA's floor is 25% of the stock's current market value, so it moves down as the price falls. Work it from the value after the drop, with the loan held fixed.

reasons: computed key (calc arith)

wrong.55%: That's the equity you start with, not how far it can fall.
wrong.25%: Used the floor as the size of the drop.
wrong.30%: Took 25 off your 55% starting equity. The floor moves down as the price falls.

find.label: Fall before the floor is hit

questions.q: The market's rolling over and you sell everything to cash. It protects you. What does it cost you?
choices: Margin interest on cash you hold
questions.why: Missing a sharp market rebound. Bear markets often end as fast as they started, with a quick rebound that's very hard to call. Sit out at the wrong time and you can miss the upswing. Idle cash also loses ground to inflation over time. So cash isn't free. It's a trade with a cost, and I take that trade on purpose when the market's weak. What it doesn't cost you is margin interest. Interest is only on money you borrow.
questions.lesson_line: Going to cash is a trade too. It has a payoff and a cost.

wrong.Margin interest on cash you hold: Interest is charged on money you borrow. Cash you hold isn't a loan.
wrong.Nothing, cash holds its value: Idle cash loses ground to inflation over time, and you can miss the upswing.
wrong.A 90-day freeze on the account: A 90-day freeze follows a rule break, such as freeriding: buying and selling before you pay. Selling shares you paid for isn't freeriding.

questions.simple: Missing a sharp rebound. Bear markets often end fast, and the turn is hard to call.

deeper.counter: Both views are real. Investopedia says the biggest risk of market timing is usually being out of the market at critical times. IBD's view: make money when the market trends higher, and protect profits when it heads lower.

reasons: Tier 2 sources only (Investopedia, Schwab); both blocked this agent on 2026-11-12, last read in context 2026-11-09

questions.story: The market is in a correction. Your last five breakouts failed within days. Few stocks are holding their moves.
questions.q: So how do you run your account right now?
choices: Go to cash and stop looking
Size up to win it back
questions.why: Raise cash and build a list. Five breakouts failing in a row is the market telling you something. In a correction most stocks follow the market down, so new buys are riskier. Even leaders can fall fast. You don't have to force anything. Cash is a position. Use the time to find the names holding up best, so you're ready when the new uptrend starts. Protect what you've got first.
questions.lesson_line: Cash is a position. In a correction, hold more of it and build your list.

wrong.Borrow to buy the dip: Corrections can keep going. Borrow into one and you can lose more than you put in.
wrong.Go to cash and stop looking: Stepping back is right. Stop looking, though, and you miss the leaders for the next uptrend.
wrong.Size up to win it back: Bigger size where most breakouts fail means bigger losses. That's how a drawdown gets deep.

questions.simple: Hold more cash and build a list of the strongest names. New buys in a correction are riskier.

deeper.trap: The trap is trying to win back losses with more size or borrowed money. A sharp correction can be disastrous for traders on heavy margin, and on margin you can lose more than you put in. Protect what you have until the market turns up.

reasons: matches the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 9, D44 and D46: cash is a position, mostly cash in a Red market); must keep teaching it

questions.q: The app's market reading is Green and you're using margin. How big can all your longs together get, as a share of the account?
questions.why: Up to 200%. When the app's market reading is Green, all your positions together can reach 200% of the account. Anything past 100% is borrowed money, and Green is the only color where we borrow. In Yellow, Orange or Red, the cap is 100%. Two things don't change on margin. Risk per trade stays a percent of the account, and one position still tops out at 40%. Borrowing makes a bad stretch hurt more, so we only do it when the market's backing our trades.

wrong.Up to 100% of the account: That's the cap when the reading isn't Green. Green is the only time we use margin.
wrong.Up to 40% of the account: 40% is our cap on one position, not all of them together.
wrong.Up to 50% of the account: That's what Regulation T lets a broker lend on a new buy. It isn't our limit on the whole book.

questions.simple: Up to 200%, using margin. Green is the only market where we borrow.
questions.lesson_line: We borrow only in a Green market. Risk per trade stays a percent of the account.

deeper.counter: The rest of this lesson shows how margin grows losses. Our rule limits it two ways: margin only in a Green market, and risk per trade stays a percent of the account.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook A7, B24 and F60, house rules that can change

conflicts: The pattern day trader rule changed this year. FINRA Regulatory Notice 26-10 (April 20, 2026) replaced the day trading margin requirements in their entirety, the four-in-five-days count and the $25,000 minimum included, effective June 4, 2026, with a phase-in for brokers until October 20, 2027. The current Rule 4210 text (version Oct 22, 2026 onwards, read 2026-11-09) has no pattern day trader provisions. Investor.gov's 'Pattern Day Trader' glossary still prints the old definition under a banner announcing the change. The plan row's practise case ('four day trades on a 20k account') assumed the old rule; the file teaches the old rule only as what a broker that has not switched may still run (w2, q17), keys the current rule as 'FINRA's rule as of November 2026' (q05, q11, q16, q19), and sets as_of 2026-11-09.

FINRA's Brokerage Accounts page, margin tip: '$25,000 ÷ (1.00 – 0.25) = $33,337'. The arithmetic gives $33,333.33. The file quotes FINRA's formula (f35) but never the $33,337 figure; q21 computes its own number through a calc.

Going to cash: IBD (CAN SLIM's M) says new buys in a correction are riskier and to protect profits when the market heads lower; Investopedia's CANSLIM and Correction pages agree that growth stocks fall when the market shifts and that buying in a correction risks a further decline. Investopedia's Market Timing and Schwab's correction pages say long-term investors usually do better staying invested, because rebounds are abrupt and hard to predict. The file asks the cash question for an active swing trader whose breakouts are failing (q23) and teaches the cost of cash from Investopedia and Schwab (q22), so both halves are shown. q23 drops a 'stay fully invested' choice, because for a long-term investor it is a defensible answer.

Good faith violation consequences ('three good faith violations in a 12-month period' then a 90-day settled-cash restriction) are Fidelity's stated practice, not a FINRA or SEC rule. FINRA defines the violation (f15) and the file keys only that; the count is named as Fidelity's in q18's why.

Selling on the settlement date itself: Fidelity's example calls it a violation to sell 'prior to Tuesday (the settlement date of the XYZ sale)', which implies a sale on Tuesday is fine, but no Tier 1 page says so outright. q14 keys 'once XYZ's sale has settled' and never asks about the settlement day itself.

Margin call size: FINRA's example sizes the call to bring equity back to the 25% minimum; brokers can ask for more (house requirements). q12 says 'using FINRA's 25% floor' so the number is FINRA's method, not any one broker's.

Checker 2026-11-09, how the new rule is watched: FINRA's Investor Insights say 'your firm monitors your account ... during the trading day', but Regulatory Notice 26-10 says real-time monitoring 'is not a requirement' and firms may make 'a single calculation' of the intraday deficit, and the same Insight says a firm may compute it 'at the end of the trading day'. The file therefore teaches that the requirement applies all day (f06, f12) and no longer says the broker checks all day (w2 changed).

w1.notes: f75 (Investor.gov Margin Account), f23, f24, f27, f30, f29 (FINRA Brokerage Accounts) and f52 (Investor.gov Margin Call) read in context on the live pages 2026-11-09; the 50% loan, the 25% floor and house levels match. Changed step 3 'you get a margin call' to 'expect a margin call': FINRA says you 'may be required' to deposit and the firm 'will likely' issue a call.

w2.notes: f45/f47 (Investor.gov glossary, old rule printed under a 2026 change banner), f01/f02 (Notice 26-10) and f06/f12/f09 (FINRA Insight) read live. Current Rule 4210 (version Oct 22, 2026 onwards) has no pattern day trader text; Notice 26-21 (Oct 2026) is about binary options and a search found no change to the phase-in, so June 4, 2026 and October 20, 2027 stand. Changed: 'four day trades' to 'four or more'; 'Your broker checks your margin all day' to 'Your equity must cover your positions all day', because Notice 26-10 lets brokers make a single end-of-day calculation (see conflicts); f12 added.

w3.notes: f39/f40 (FINRA Understanding Settlement Cycles, May 7, 2026: the first plain fetch got a 429, a second fetch and WebFetch both showed the text), f15 (FINRA Frequent Intraday Trading, June 4, 2026) and f49/f50 (Investor.gov Freeriding) read in context. Tuesday sale settling Wednesday is FINRA's own example; the 90-day freeze is the SEC page's 'may require ... freeze'.

q02.notes: Blunt opener, practical how (watch your equity yourself). Facts f30/f31/f52/f53 match.

q03.notes: Stem read like a glossary prompt ('Tap the number FINRA sets as the least equity'). Rewritten as a trader holding margin asking how low equity can go. Why and simple were fine; 25% and 50% both cited.

q04.notes: Verdict first, '50% to get in, 25% to stay in' is a line he'd say. Numbers right.

q05.notes: Keys the current rule (June 4, 2026; phase-in to October 20, 2027) and tells you to ask your broker. Correct per the conflicts note.

q06.notes: Thursday to Friday on T+1 is right; T+2 would be Monday. Says why a cash trader cares.

q07.notes: Fine voice; 'That stock' had no referent. Stem now names a stock on your list.

q08.notes: Options T+1 per f41/f34. Plain and practical.

q09.notes: Math right: 12,500 - 10,000 = 2,500; 2,500 / 12,500 = 0.2. Truth tweak: 'you're getting a margin call' overstated it; FINRA says the firm will likely call (the walkthrough checker made the same change), so 'expect a margin call'.

q10.notes: The A-then-B chain is right (f58). Gives the fix: hold B or pay with settled cash.

q11.notes: $2,000 to borrow (f10/f18), under it cash only (f11), $25,000 was the old PDT line. Correct.

q12.notes: Shows the steps: 25% of 24,000 = 6,000; 24,000 - 20,000 = 4,000; gap 2,000. Mentor line about being that close to the line. Paying 2,000 cash does land exactly on the floor (equity 6,000 on 24,000).

q13.notes: 20,000 x 30% = 6,000; 6,000 / 10,000 = 0.6. 'The stock fell 30% and you lost 60%. That's margin.' is his register.

q14.notes: Truth fine (Tuesday, f57). The 'Fidelity's own example is this exact trade' line read like a research note in the why; replaced with the stop-versus-violation situation spelled out and the practical fix.

q19.notes: Correct but a list of facts. Rewritten with a concrete midday-flush picture and what to do. Does not claim the broker monitors in real time (conflicts note), only that the requirement covers the whole day (f12).

q20.notes: 35% against a new 40% house level, call right away (f27/f28/f32). Practical: leave room on volatile names.

q21.notes: Steps shown: 9,000 / 0.75 = 12,000; 20,000 - 12,000 = 8,000; 8,000 / 20,000 = 0.4. Wrong notes match real mistakes (55% start equity, 55 - 25 = 30).
